title: "Home Exercise"

## Instructions

::: callout-note
This exercise is ungraded practice - you don't need to submit it. But it's the best preparation for the reports and the exam, so do try to complete it.
:::

The at-home exercises should be completed using Posit cloud, Home Exercise 8. Create a new .Rmd file (use File -\> New File -\> R Markdown).

I advise saving the new file straight away, and regularly re-save it.

When you have finished the exercise (or part of it), 'knit' the file to check that it works.

Before you begin, load the following packages at the top of your markdown document, and download the world map:

```{r}
#| eval: false

library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(rnaturalearth)

worldmap <- ne_countries(scale = 'medium', returnclass = 'sf')
```

## Tasks

These tasks practise everything from [Your first map](43_first-map.qmd) and [Map projections](44_projections.qmd). For each one, write a sentence explaining what you're doing, followed by the code.

1.  Make a map of the countries of Asia. Use `coord_sf()` to zoom in so there's no unnecessary empty space.

2.  The world map has a column `gdp_md`, containing each country's GDP (the total value of its economy) in millions of US dollars. Use `mutate()` to make a new column containing the **GDP per person** (remember that `gdp_md` is in *millions* of dollars, and population is in `pop_est`). Watch out: missing values in this dataset are recorded as `-99`, so filter out any negative GDP values first.

3.  Make a map of the whole world (without Antarctica), with each country filled by GDP per person. Then:

    -   Use an equal-area projection.
    -   Choose a suitable colour scale, and give the legend a clear title.
    -   Give the borders a colour and width that make the map easy to read.
    -   Add a title, subtitle, and a caption giving the source of the data.
    -   Use `theme_void()`.

4.  Make a second version of the same map, this time filling the countries by **total GDP** instead of GDP per person. Write a few sentences comparing the two maps: what does each one show, and which would you use to compare how wealthy people are in different countries? Why?

5.  In a few sentences, reflect on the data: where does it come from (look at the [Natural Earth](https://www.naturalearthdata.com/) website), and what can't a map of GDP tell you?

6.  **Optional challenge:** make a map of Europe in the projection with the EPSG code 3035, with each country filled by its `income_grp`, and the countries outside Europe drawn in light grey.
